questions.question: What is the core problem with textbook RSA encryption (c = m^e mod n) used directly on message integers?
options: It is deterministic and malleable, so it lacks semantic security and integrity.
It is too slow, so attackers can brute-force the private key by timing it.
It produces ciphertexts longer than the modulus, so decryption fails randomly.
It only works for prime moduli, so it breaks for composite n.
questions.explanation: Without a padding scheme, RSA is a deterministic algebraic function and attackers can test equality or transform ciphertexts into related ciphertexts.

questions.question: What does MGF1 do in OAEP and PSS?
options: Expands a seed into a pseudorandom mask of a requested length using a hash function.
Generates RSA primes by repeatedly hashing random bytes until a prime appears.
Makes RSA exponentiation constant-time by blinding the base and exponent.
Compresses long messages so they fit into a single RSA block.
questions.explanation: MGF1 is a hash-based expander: it deterministically turns a seed into as many mask bytes as you need.

questions.question: OAEP message length limit: for modulus length k bytes and hash output length hLen bytes, what is the maximum message length OAEP can encode?
options: k - 2*hLen - 2 bytes
k - hLen - 2 bytes
k - 2*hLen bytes
k - 11 bytes
questions.explanation: OAEP requires space for lHash (hLen), seed (hLen), separators, and structure: mLen <= k - 2*hLen - 2.

questions.question: In OAEP decoding, what must be checked to reject malformed blocks (beyond “it decrypts”)?
options: The lHash matches Hash(label), then a 0x01 separator appears after only zero bytes.
The ciphertext is odd and ends with 0xbc, otherwise it is invalid.
The decrypted integer is divisible by e, otherwise it is invalid.
The message starts with ASCII and contains no zero bytes.
questions.explanation: OAEP defines a strict byte structure; decoding re-derives masks, unmasks, and validates lHash and the 0x01 separator placement.

questions.question: Why does RSASSA-PSS use emBits = nBits - 1 instead of nBits when building the encoded message EM?
options: To guarantee OS2IP(EM) is in range (< n) without relying on chance.
Because RSA can only sign odd integers and emBits enforces oddness.
To make signatures one byte shorter for bandwidth savings.
Because the final byte 0xbc consumes one bit of capacity.
questions.explanation: PSS clears the leftmost bits so the encoded message representative is safely below n; the spec defines emBits = nBits - 1.

questions.question: You are using RSAES-OAEP with SHA-256. Which MGF1 choice is the right default unless an interop spec says otherwise?
options: MGF1 with SHA-256 (same hash as OAEP)
MGF1 with SHA-1 (legacy default, always safe)
MGF1 with SHA-512 (stronger, so always better)
No MGF1: replace it with raw random bytes
questions.explanation: OAEP security and interop depend on parameter coupling; the standard default is to use the same hash for Hash and MGF1.

questions.question: Why is PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption (RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5) considered dangerous in many protocols even though it is randomized?
options: Padding validity can leak via error behavior (padding oracles), enabling chosen-ciphertext attacks.
It always reuses the same padding bytes, so ciphertexts repeat.
It requires a secret label value that many systems accidentally log.
It cannot be implemented with big integers, so it overflows.
questions.explanation: Bleichenbacher-style attacks exploit differences in how implementations report or handle malformed v1.5 padding.

questions.question: What is the correct high-level flow for verifying an RSA-PSS signature?
options: Compute mHash = Hash(message), recover EM = S^e mod n, then run PSS verification on EM against mHash.
Decrypt the signature with the private key, then compare to the message bytes directly.
Hash the signature and compare it to Hash(message) to avoid expensive RSA.
Verify the signature by checking whether it is a prime number.
questions.explanation: Verification uses the public exponent to recover the encoded message EM and then checks the PSS structure against Hash(message).
